Vertical Competition on a Common Platform

Xiaojuan Puyang Sichuan Normal University, Chengdu, Sichuan, China, jxpuyang@sicnu.edu.cn

Jane Gu University of Connecticut, jane.gu@uconn.edu

Rachel R. Chen University of California, Davis, rachen@ucdavis.edu

Juan Li Nanjing University, juanli@nju.edu.cn

We consider a platform whose infrastructure constitutes common attributes for vertically differentiated

products in a digital goods market. We examine how vendors craft individual attributes of their products,

and how the platform decides on the provision and pricing of its infrastructure when facing vendors’ strate-

gic reactions. First, we find that when the platform offers more powerful infrastructure, the high-quality

vendor improves individual attributes, whereas its low-quality rival reduces individual attributes, exhibiting

a pattern of divergence. On the other hand, when the platform charges a higher commission rate for using its

infrastructure, both vendors slash individual attributes, with the high-quality vendor slashing more. Second,

we find that when vendors’ development cost declines but remains high, the platform improves infrastructure

and reduces the commission rate. But when vendors’ development cost is already low and keeps declining,

the platform scales back in infrastructure but still reduces the commission rate. Finally, we show the strate-

gic response of the platform, when coupled with vendors’ improved product development efficiency, further

boost the platform profit, both vendors’ profits, and consumer surplus, leading to a win-win-win outcome.

Key words : common attributes, vertical competition, platform infrastructure, game theory

1. Introduction

Vendors competing to sell through a common platform face unique opportunities and challenges.

On the one hand, the platform, typically a digital marketplace or service hub, provides common

infrastructure that streamlines vendors’ development process, ensures consistency in user interface,

and so enhances user experience with vendors’ products. For example, Steam.com, the largest online

platform where users buy, play, create and discuss PC games, is known for its easiness of use.1 As

one of Steam users commented: “You can add mods to your game with a simple click, and you

(usually) don’t have to toy with the game files to get them to work. No other desktop client makes

it this easy to make, download, or install mods for your games.”2 Apple’s iOS supports a large

number of app developers with tools and resources that facilitate the distribution and monetization

of apps.3 On the other hand, competing vendors operating on the shared ecosystem strive to

differentiate. For instance, high-quality note-taking apps on iOS such as GoodNotes offer polished

interfaces with advanced features such as handwriting recognition and cloud sync,4 whereas lower-

quality options, such as Note-Ify or Evernote, fall short in these areas.5 Premium video games

released on Steam.com such as Skyrim and Red Dead Redemption compete by providing a polished,

immersive experience that their low-quality counterparts can hardly match. Such quality variance

is also reflected in game ratings (from no review to 95% positive reviews).6

For competing vendors, the platform infrastructure provides the “common attributes” that are

indispensable and inseparable from their products. Consumers’ perceived value of a vendor prod-

uct (e.g., a video game on Steam.com) not only stems from the product’s individual attributes

but also depends on the common infrastructure (e.g., platform reliability). Technology platforms

Author: Article Short Title 3

are also known to invest heavily in enhancing their infrastructure. For example, Steam.com con-

stantly announces updates in developer tools,7 which help developers enhance game development,

marketing, and user engagement. Because common attributes from the platform constitute an

indispensable part of product values, their changes will shake the balance of competition in a verti-

cally differentiated market. In particular, vendors that target the high-end market and the low-end

market may take different reactions in adjusting individual attributes of their products, which have

implications for their pricing, competition outcome, and consumer welfare. Yet changes in common

attributes shared by horizontally differentiated products do not affect their relative values and so

are unlikely to induce asymmetric responses from vendors. In this study, we theorize how common

attributes provided by a platform affect vertical competition in a digital goods market.

In practice, a platform typically monetizes its infrastructure provision by charging vendors a

transaction-based commission (Borck et al. 2020). For example, Steam.com takes a 30% commission

on sales made through its platform, including video games, downloadable content, or other virtual

goods sold within games.8 The commission can be viewed as the price vendors pay for using the

infrastructure. Naturally, a platform’s commission rate will interact with its infrastructure provision

to affect vendor competition.

Moreover, a strategic platform can benefit from adjusting the provision and pricing of common

infrastructure when facing changes in vendor productivity. For instance, third-party GenAI tools

such as Promethean AI, Meshy.ai, and Rosebud AI can help game developers enhance gameplay

mechanics, improve storytelling and animation, and streamline development processes,9 lifting

productivity for all vendors on Steam.com. Such universal improvement in vendor productivity

reshapes vendors’ competition as well as the platform’s strategy to profit from the vendor market.

Aiming at understanding the strategic implications of a platform’s common infrastructure in

a vertically differentiated market, we ask the following research questions: 1) How would high-

4 Author: Article Short Title

and low-quality vendors adjust their products’ individual attributes and pricing, in response to

advancement in platform infrastructure or a higher commission rate for using the platform? 2)

Considering vendors’ strategic reactions, how should a platform decide its offering of common

infrastructure and the corresponding commission rate? 3) Should the platform expand or scale

back its infrastructure to take advantage of enhanced productivity of vendors, and how would it

adjust the corresponding commission rate?

To address these research questions, we model a platform whose infrastructure (e.g., user inter-

face, reliable payment, and order fulfillment) constitutes common attributes for vertically differ-

entiated products in a digital goods market. The platform collects a commission for each unit of

vendor product sales. After the platform sets the infrastructure and commission rate, competing

vendors decide individual attributes as well as product prices to maximize profit.

Our investigation reveals how advances in platform infrastructure affect vendors’ vertical compe-

tition. Conventional wisdom suggests that vendors will slash individual attributes to take advantage

of the enhancement in common attributes, a substitution effect. Surprisingly, we find that although

the low-quality vendor reduces individual attributes, the high-quality vendor in this case increases

its individual attributes instead. This happens because more desirable common attributes exert a

“bottom-up” influence, with a stronger impact on the low-quality vendor than on the high-quality

vendor. The competition status of the low-quality vendor is strengthened as a result, providing

incentive for the high-quality vendor to position away from its rival by elevating its individual

attributes. We find that for digital goods with trivial marginal cost, this incentive is strong enough

to dominate the substitution effect.10 On the other hand, a higher commission rate discourages both

vendors from offering individual attributes in a “top-down” pattern. In particular, the high-quality

vendor reduces individual attributes in a greater magnitude than its low-quality rival. Accordingly,

both vendors slash their prices in spite of the higher commission rate, and sell to more consumers.

We then investigate the platform’s decisions related to the provision and pricing (i.e., the com-

mission rate) of its infrastructure when considering vendors’ strategic reactions. Intuitively, the

10 For products with substantial marginal cost, the substitution effect may dominate (proof available upon request).

Author: Article Short Title 5

platform will offer better infrastructure if doing so becomes more cost-effective. We thus focus our

investigation on an interesting scenario when technology advancements in the vendors’ industry

reduce their product development costs and consequently incentivize them to offer better individ-

ual attributes. We find that when vendors’ development cost becomes lower, the platform first

improves, and then reduces its infrastructure, following a non-monotonic pattern. Nonetheless,

the platform lowers its commission rate always. These strategic activities benefit the platform

by influencing the vendors’ incentive to enhance individual attributes. Specifically, the platform’s

responses boost the increase in individual attributes for the high-quality vendor when vendors’

product development efficiency improves but remains low, and boost the increase in individual

attributes for the low-quality vendor when such efficiency is already high.

Finally, we find the strategic response of the platform, when coupled with the technology advance-

ment of vendors, leads to a win-win-win outcome for all market players. Not only does the platform

improve profit from its strategic move, but both vendors also obtain greater profits and consumers

obtain greater total surplus. This result highlights the critical role of technology platforms in sup-

porting the digital economy as the providers of common infrastructure. Furthermore, we explore

the scenario where the platform, in addition to collecting commission income, also benefits from

inducing a higher sales volume. We find that a platform that receives mixed income always charges

a higher commission rate, compared to the case when it receives commission income only.

In summary, this paper examines the strategic implications of platform infrastructure on ver-

tical vendor competition in a digital goods market. We contribute by theorizing how common

attributes affect competing vendors’ quality and pricing decisions. Our analyses reveal the asym-

metric responses of vertically differentiated firms11 in their crafting of individual attributes when

common attributes become more appealing, along with the strategic implications of firms’ strategic

reactions on market competition and consumer welfare. Understanding the impact of enhanced

common attributes is particularly important in our research context of digital goods market, where

11 Throughout the paper, we use the terms “firms” and “vendors” interchangeably.

the trivial marginal cost leads to fierce competition and allows the high-quality firm to enjoy

dominating power (Jones and Mendelson 2011). As such, our results shed lights on how platform

infrastructure shapes vertical competition in a digital goods market.

This paper also offers timely insights into today’s market environment where firms increasingly

depend on common infrastructure provided by powerful digital platforms for their operations. Such

platforms help small vendors develop and distribute innovative products, which otherwise would be

unable to survive due to the lack of resources for mass advertising. We show that facing improved

product development efficiency in the vendor industry, a strategic platform benefits from tailoring

its offering of common infrastructure and commission rate to support and boost vendors’ incentive

to enhance products’ individual attributes. The resulting win-win-win outcome from the platform’s

strategic response points to how the growth of technology platforms helps fuel the digital economy.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We review related literature in Section 2 and

set up the model in Section 3. In Section 4, we analyze the subgame of vendor competition and the

platform’s strategies. In Section 5, we demonstrate the robustness of the key results, which helps

deepen our understanding of the underlying drives of the main model. Section 6 concludes.

2. Literature Review

Our work is related to two streams of literature: common attributes in vertical competition and

platform provision of infrastructure, which we discuss in turn.

Common Attributes in Vertical Competition

Early studies on common attributes have largely focused on monopoly settings where multiple

products offered by a monopolist share common manufacturing technologies (e.g., both Lexus and

Avalon ride on the same chassis). For example, researchers have examined product line configura-

tion when adopting common components can lower manufacturing costs (Kim and Chhajed 2000,

Desai et al. 2001, Krishnan and Gupta 2001, Heese and Swaminathan 2006). Research on com-

mon attributes shared by competing firms is scant, with the exception of Ke and Lin (2020). This

work considers common attributes shared by horizontally differentiated products and examines

Page 7

Author: Article Short Title 7

competing firms’ pricing decisions when product qualities are exogenously given but unknown to

consumers. In this setting, changes in common attributes have symmetric impacts on competing

firms. In contrast, our study considers common attributes shared by vertically differentiated prod-

ucts and examines competing firms’ quality as well as pricing decisions. In this vertical competition

context, changes in common attributes exert a “bottom-up” influence, with a stronger impact on

the low-quality firm than on the high-quality firm.

By investigating how common attributes affect vertical competition, our study contributes to the

extensive literature on firms’ quality choices under vertical differentiation (e.g., Mussa and Rosen

1978, Bonanno 1986, Gabszewicz et al. 1986). The majority of this research considers product

markets where the firm incurs substantial marginal production cost (e.g., material, labor) (e.g.,

Shaked and Sutton 1982, Moorthy 1984, 1988, Chambers et al. 2006, Shugan et al. 2017). In

contrast, our analysis focuses on digital goods markets characterized by trivial marginal cost, and we

observe the interesting finding that the high-quality firm increases individual attributes in response

to more desirable common attributes. Shugan et al. (2017) examines a monopoly firm’s decision

about whether to bundle a core product with an add-on in a product line when the quality of

the core product and the add-on are both endogenously determined. We instead consider common

attributes that are intrinsic and inseparable from the product (e.g., technology infrastructure).

A few existing works examine vertical competitive markets where the firm incurs negligible

marginal production cost relative to development cost (e.g., Lehmann-Grube 1997, Wei and Nault

2014). The literature shows that when marginal cost is trivial, price discrimination is not profitable

so that a monopolist will only offer one product instead of a product line (e.g., Anderson and

Dana 2009, Bhargava and Choudhary 2008). Jones and Mendelson (2011) further considers duopoly

competition and shows that trivial marginal cost leads to high level of market concentration, where

the high-quality firm has dominating power over the low-quality firm. In contrast, in a regular

goods market with substantial marginal cost, the high-quality and the low-quality firms have more

balanced market power. Amacher et al. (2005) compares social welfare optimum and duopoly

Page 8

8 Author: Article Short Title

equilibrium for markets with negligible or substantial marginal costs, respectively. Our study adds

to this research by investigating how competing vendors devise individual attributes in response

to common platform infrastructure.

Our study is related to the broad literature on information goods, which are known to have trivial

marginal cost. The majority of this research examines demand-side characteristics of information

goods, such as low cost of sharing (Varian 2000, Bakos et al. 1999, Galbreth et al. 2012) and

prevalence of product renting (Sundararajan 2004, Balasubramanian et al. 2015, Choudhary 2010).

Our study adds to the stream of research that examines supply-side characteristics of information

goods, i.e., trivial marginal cost. For example, Bakos and Brynjolfsson (1999) and Bakos and

Brynjolfsson (2000) consider how the trivial marginal cost of information goods can affect bundling

strategies. We show that the trivial marginal cost plays a major role on how common attributes

affect vertical competition.

Platform Provision of Infrastructure

Our study examines how a platform decides the provision and pricing of its infrastructure by

considering their implications for vendor competition. A body of literature considers a two-sided

platform’s decision on its own performance (“quality”) level that may affect user participation.

Anderson et al. (2014) recognizes that, in cases such as video game platforms, even though superior

platform performance such as improved graphics is a selling point for consumers, the level of tech-

nological complexity may increase game development costs and thus discourage the entry of game

developers. Tan et al. (2020) examines the choice of direct investments that increase participation

on both sides of the platform and interact with its two-sided pricing decisions. Casadesus-Masanell

and Llanes (2015) studies incentives to invest in platform quality in open-source and proprietary

two-sided platforms. Whereas this literature abstracts away vendor competition, we model compet-

ing vendors that decide individual attributes and pricing for vertically differentiated products in

response to platform infrastructure and show how vendor’s strategic reactions drive the platform’s

infrastructure provision and pricing strategies.

Page 9

Author: Article Short Title 9

With a focus on vendor quality competition, our analysis is related to the emerging literature

on quality regulation and infrastructure provision by platforms. To regulate vendors’ quality, the

platform could use an exclusion strategy (Hagiu 2009, Zheng and Kaiser 2013), a first-party appli-

cations strategy where the platform becomes vertically integrated (Hagiu and Spulber 2013, Lee

2013), and a subsidization strategy (Huang et al. 2022). The aforementioned works consider the

quality of upstream vendors as exogenously given. In our study, vendors endogenously determine

their individual attributes, and the common infrastructure provided by the platform is an integral

part of the product value to consumers.

Broadly speaking, our study relates to the extensive research investigating how a major retailer

induces strategic responses of upstream manufacturers. Researchers have investigated manufacturer

strategies such as information sharing (Gal-Or et al. 2008), assortment (e.g., Dukes et al. 2009,

Inderst and Shaffer 2007), product specification (e.g., Luo et al. 2007, Dukes et al. 2014), wholesale

prices (Gu and Liu 2013), and retail prices (e.g., Chen 2003, Marx and Shaffer 2007, Raju and

Zhang 2005). These studies typically consider a wholesale price contract between manufacturers and

the big retailer, where the retailer benefits from intensified manufacturer competition. In contrast,

our study considers a revenue-sharing scheme between the platform and vendors, in which case

the platform’s incentive to maximize commission income aligns with vendors’ incentive to enhance

sales revenue. Previous research has examined the interactions between the platform and vendors

on a revenue-sharing contract, including information asymmetry (Bart et al. 2021), the nature

of bargaining (MacDonald and Ryall 2004, Oh et al. 2015), how platforms squeeze the surplus

from vendors (Balseiro et al. 2017), product recommendations (Li et al. 2018, 2020, Zhou and Zou

2023), and differential commission rates (Bhargava et al. 2022). Most studies on revenue sharing in

platform context assume that vendor qualities are exogenously given (e.g., Jiang et al. 2011, Ryan

et al. 2012, Abhishek et al. 2016, Ha et al. 2022). Hsiao et al. (2024) consider endogenous quality

decisions of competing manufacturers who decide on their product quality before the platform

chooses its commission rate.

Page 10

10 Author: Article Short Title

Recent studies compare the revenue-sharing contract with other contracts on a retail platform.

They use numerical simulations to explore endogenous quality decisions of competing manufactur-

ers after the platform sets the commission rate (Zhang et al. 2019, Xiong et al. 2024). Differently,

in our research context, the platform infrastructure constitutes the common attributes that are

indispensable and inseparable from vendors’ products, and the commission rate can be viewed

as the price for using such infrastructure. We characterize how the platform jointly decides its

infrastructure provision and commission rate, and how these decisions affect competing vendors in

setting their individual attributes.

3. Model Setup

We consider a platform that provides infrastructure to two competing firms, each selling a single

product to consumers.

Platform The platform’s infrastructure constitutes common attributes of products offered by

vendors. Let E ≥0 denote the value of common attributes, a summary measure for all more-is-

better attributes shared by both products. For example, online video game platform Steam.com

provides a powerful infrastructure that allows for smooth experiences for users to make, download

or install mods for their games. The platform experience together with a game’s playing features

constitutes consumers’ perceived value of the game. This is consistent with the notion that a prod-

uct sold online can be viewed as a bundle of the core product (e.g., the product’s key features) and

the extended product (e.g., service provided by the online seller) (Ba and Pavlou 2002, Dellarocas

2003). In such a market environment, changes in platform infrastructure may induce a vendor

to alter its quality provision, which is similar to the practice where vendors alter their products

for different sales channels.12 The platform incurs a cost λE2

Author: Article Short Title 11

λ ≥0 is the cost coefficient. A higher value of λ indicates a higher cost for the platform to provide

infrastructure.

The platform charges a commission for its provision of common infrastructure. Following the

widely used revenue-sharing scheme (e.g., Chen et al. 2016, Bhargava et al. 2022), we assume that

the platform collects a portion α of the total revenue and each vendor keeps (1 −α) portion of its

own revenue, α ∈[0,1]. For instance, Steam.com takes a 30% cut of the revenue generated from

game sales, downloadable content, and in-game purchases.13 We assume that α is industry-specific

and thus the same for both vendors. If a vendor pays the platform for additional, customized

services, such payment can be viewed as the vendor’s cost of improving its individual attributes.

Vendors We consider a product equilibrium in which the vendors offer different levels of indi-

vidual attributes qH and qL, respectively, with qH > qL ≥0. That is, we look for an equilibrium in

which the vendors offer different levels of individual attributes. Otherwise, if they choose the same

individual attributes, fierce competition will force both firms to price at unit cost, leading to a dom-

inated equilibrium where both firms earn negative profits (Jones and Mendelson 2011, Lin 2017). In

our research context of digital goods, the marginal cost is typically trivial. We thus assume that for

individual attributes qi (i = H,L), firm i incurs zero marginal cost and an overall development cost

Game Sequence The game has three stages: In stage 1, the platform decides E and α. In stage 2,

competing vendors simultaneously choose individual attributes qH and qL. In stage 3, both vendors

simultaneously choose product prices pH and pL; consumers make purchase decisions.

4. Analysis

We solve the game backwards. §4.1 derives the subgame equilibrium of vendor competition, given

the platform’s infrastructure provision E and commission rate α. §4.2 then explores the platform’s

optimal strategies.

4.1. Subgame of Vendor Competition

In this subgame, each vendor decides its individual attributes and price, taking the platform’s

common attributes E and commission rate α as given. Let θHL denote the type of the threshold

consumer who is indifferent between purchasing product L and product H, i.e., θHL(qH +E)−pH =

θHL(qL +E)−pL. Similarly, θL0 denotes the type of threshold consumer who is indifferent between

purchasing product L and not purchasing at all, i.e., θL0(qL +E)−pL = 0. From the two equations,

we obtain:

When common attributes become more desirable, one might expect vendors to slash their indi-

vidual attributes so as to enjoy a cost reduction. However, Proposition 1(i) shows diverging trends

in competing vendors’ individual attributes as common attributes become more desirable. As illus-

trated in Figure 1, facing a rise in E, vendor H responds by improving qH whereas vendor L

responds by cutting qL. This is because improved infrastructure by allowing vendor L to expand

demand to the low-end market helps enhance vendor L’s competition status against vendor H,

suggesting a “bottom-up” impact. In our research context of digital goods, such intensified com-

petition gives vendor H strong incentive to increase individual attributes and position away from

vendor L. Below we detail this insight by identifying two routes through which a higher E affects

competing vendors’ individual attribute decisions.

Figure 1: Impact of Common Attributes on Individual Attributes (f = 0.4)

First route: This route of impact comes from two effects of E.

Page 15

Author: Article Short Title 15

Low-end expansion effect To see this effect, consider the case when both firms’ individual

attributes and prices are fixed. In this case, a larger E increases consumer utility for product H

and product L by the same amount and therefore have no bearing on a consumer’s preference

when choosing between the two products. Meanwhile, more desirable common attributes favor the

purchasing decision and convert some consumers at the low end of the market from non-buyers

to buyers of product L. Similar low-end expansion effects can be observed in prior research that

considers a partially covered market (e.g., Moorthy 1988, Jones and Mendelson 2011, Jing 2007).

Surplus extraction effect To see this effect, consider the case when vendors are able to adjust

prices but individual attributes are fixed. In this case, a larger E motivates both vendors to raise

their prices, but the low-end expansion effect gives vendor L more room to do so. This is because

any increase in pH will result in pure demand loss for firm H, whereas firm L can offset such

demand loss by acquiring new buyers from the low-end market.15 This additional flexibility in

pricing enhances vendor L’s competition status, as reflected by the reduced price gap between pH

and pL (see equation (8)).

These two effects, when combined, form the first route of impact on vendors’ individual attributes

decisions. In particular, the reduced price gap suggests intensified competition, which encourages

firms to position away from each other once they are able to do so (e.g., Shaked and Sutton 1982,

Moorthy 1988). Importantly, the impact through this route is particularly strong for digital goods,

for which the fierce price competition due to trivial marginal cost (Jones and Mendelson 2011)

motivates firm L to slash qL, but pushes firm H to increase qH.

Second route: This route of impact comes from the following effect.

Quality substitution effect If firms can adjust individual attributes but not prices, more desirable

common attributes naturally induce them to slash their individual offerings. This effect is similar to

what is demonstrated in Desai (2001), Geng et al. (2022), and Lambertini and Orsini (2001) where

positive externality by enhancing product valuations motivates firms to reduce quality provision.

Intuitively, this effect becomes weaker under lower marginal production cost.

15 In contrast, for horizontally differentiated firms, common attributes have symmetric impacts on firm pricing.

Page 16

16 Author: Article Short Title

Whereas the three effects exist separately in other settings, our study provides an interesting

context where all three are present. Because their impacts on the vendors’ product decisions are not

always aligned, it is unclear which effect(s) dominates at the equilibrium. Proposition 1 answers this

exact question, which is new to the literature. Specifically, for digital goods with trivial marginal

cost, the substitution effect is weak and so the impact of E through the second route is dominated

by the first route of impact.16 This leads to the divergence of the vendors’ individual attributes

as illustrated in Figure 1. In contrast, in markets where the marginal cost is substantial, the

substitution effect becomes much stronger and could dominate the impact of the first route, so that

firm H may reduce its individual attributes as E increases. We have conducted numerical analysis

to verify this insight.

Note that more desirable common attributes increase the overall quality of both products in

equilibrium with widened quality gap, which ultimately expands the price gap as indicated in

Proposition 1(ii). This equilibrium result contrasts equation (8), which shows a reduced price gap

if vendors do not adjust individual attributes in response to more desirable common attributes.

This contrast highlights how vendors’ strategic adjustment of individual attributes helps alleviate

competition pressure.

We next investigate how common attributes affect equilibrium outcome. Intuitively, when com-

mon attributes become more desirable, both firms and consumers are better off. We define profit

ratio πL/(πL + πH), which indicates firm L’s competition status relative to firm H, and derive

consumers’ total surplus as follows.

Corollary 1(i) shows that, when common attributes become more desirable, in equilibrium the

demand expands not only for firm L, but for firm H as well. That is, more low-end consumers are

served, and some consumers will upgrade from product L to product H.

Interestingly, Corollary 1(ii) reveals asymmetric impacts of improved common attributes on firm

profits—firm L experiences a higher percentage increase in profit than firm H. This suggests an

improvement of firm L’s competitive status, or softened market dominance of firm H. Figure 2(a)

illustrates this result, i.e., πL/(πH +πL) increases with E from 5.9% (when E = 0) to 19.37% (when

E reaches the upper bound, beyond which qL ≤0).17 This is consistent with the “bottom-up” effect

revealed by Proposition 1, which shows that common attributes more directly affect the low-quality

firm than the high-quality firm, and consequently improve its profit share.

Note that improved common attributes not only improve the overall quality consumers enjoy,

but also expand the market coverage, both contributing to higher consumer welfare. Corollary

Proposition 2(i) shows that a higher commission rate leads to lower quality provision of both

vendors, which confirms the numerical findings for a retail platform (Zhang et al. 2019, Xiong et al.

2024). More importantly, our analysis reveals that in response to a higher commission rate, the

high-quality vendor experiences a more pronounced reduction in individual attributes. As such, the

commission rate exhibits a “top-down” pattern of influence, which poses an interesting contrast

to the “bottom-up” influence brought by common attributes as shown in Corollary 1. Intuitively,

the high-quality firm that dominates the market relinquishes a greater volume of profit than the

low-quality firm when facing the shift in commission rate, and so adjusts its offering in a larger

magnitude.

Conventional wisdom suggests that a higher commission rate will drive vendors to charge higher

prices. Nonetheless, the higher commission rate also incentivizes vendors to cut down individual

attributes, and consequently creates a downward pressure on prices. As shown in Proposition 2(ii)

and (iii), the decline in prices prevails, resulting in higher demands for both vendors.

The result above highlights how the platform can use commission rate in addition to infrastruc-

ture provision to influence vendors’ product strategies. We next examine the platform strategies.

Lemma 2 suggests that the platform’s optimal commission rate α∗is uniquely determined by the

Intuitively, a higher cost for building the infrastructure (i.e., a higher λ) suppresses the platform’s

provision of common attributes, which subsequently impacts the vendors’ individual attributes and

prices as identified in §4.1. It is, however, interesting to investigate how the platform chooses E and

With the decline of product development cost f, vendors are incentivized to provide higher

individual attributes. In this case, one might expect that the platform slashes its infrastructure.

Also, it is intuitive that the platform could raise its commission rate to take advantage of the

efficiency gain of vendors’ market. Surprisingly, Proposition 3 shows that the adjustment of the

infrastructure is not monotone with the decline in vendors’ development cost. Result (i) shows that

when vendors’ development cost f is reduced but remains relatively high, the platform invests more

to improve its infrastructure, suggesting that the platform’s benefit from the enhanced revenue

in the vendors’ market more than compensates for the higher cost of infrastructure improvement.

However, if vendors’ cost f is already very small and continues to decline, the platform prefers to

reduce provision of infrastructure to save cost.

Meanwhile, Proposition 3(ii) shows the platform always accommodates a reduced product devel-

opment cost of vendors with a lowered commission rate. This implies as vendors become more

efficient in developing individual attributes, they will be taxed less by the platform, which conse-

quently motivates vendors to provide better individual attributes as indicated by Proposition 2. As

such, a positive feedback loop is instigated. We illustrate this result in Figure 3, where f declines

along the horizontal axis from the right to the left.

Page 21

Author: Article Short Title 21

Proposition 3 highlights the importance for the platform to consider the impact of its infrastruc-

ture and commission rate on vendors’ individual attribute decisions. With the vendor technology

improvement such as GenAI, the platform needs to carefully craft its response by adjusting the

infrastructure and the commission rate simultaneously. This insight is elaborated in the next corol-

lary, which shows the quality boosting impact of a strategic platform.

Figure 3: Platform’s optimal Provision of Common Attributes and Commission Rate

Corollary 2 (Quality boosting impact of strategic platform). When vendors’ develop-

ment cost coefficient f declines, both qH and qL increase. Moreover, there exists a threshold f

(higher than f), so that the platform’s strategic decisions on E and α boost the increase of qH when

f > f, and boost the increase of qL otherwise.

Intuitively, both vendors will increase individual attributes when f becomes smaller. Corollary

2 shows that the platform’s strategic response to vendors’ lower development cost may bring an

additional, indirect boost on their individual attributes. Interestingly, the manifestation of the

boosting effect depends on the region of development cost f.

When f declines but remains above f, then f > f so that the platform responds with higher

infrastructure E, but surprisingly charges a lower commission rate α (see Proposition 3). In this

region, the low quality firm’s incentive to raise its individual attributes due to a reduced product

development cost is inhibited by the competition pressure from the high-quality firm. The increased

Page 22

22 Author: Article Short Title

E and reduced α together always boost qH, but may boost or suppress qL at the same time (Recall

Proposition 1 shows that higher E results in higher qH and lower qL, whereas Proposition 2 shows

that lower α results in higher qH and qL). The additional boost in qH allows firm H to charge a

higher price while alleviating competition pressure for firm L, both effects benefiting the platform.

On the other hand, when f is below f and continues to decline, the platform reduces E and

correspondingly charges a lower commission rate α. In this region, qH is already very high, suggest-

ing limited room for further enhancement. As a result, the platform finds it optimal to focus on

boosting qL, and the reduced E and α both serve this purpose. The further increase in qL leads to a

higher price for firm L, which makes product L less attractive and alleviates competition pressure

for firm H. Both effects benefit the platform. Lastly, our analysis shows that this strategy holds

optimal even when f < f < f (see proof of Corollary 2 for details).

Intuitively, when vendors’ technology advancement brings down their development cost, the

improved efficiency makes all market players better off, increasing platform payoff ΠP, vendor

profits πL and πH, and consumer surplus CS. Our next proposition shows that the platform’s

strategic response to the decline of f further enhances social welfare.

Proposition 4 (Strategic response of platform). When vendors’ development cost coeffi-

cient f declines, the strategic response of the platform leads to higher profits of vendors and the

platform, as well as a higher consumer welfare.

Proposition 4 highlights how strategic response of the platform, when coupled with a reduced

development cost in the vendors’ industry, brings a win-win-win outcome to all players in the

market. Whereas the platform adjusts E and α to maximize its own payoff, such adjustments help

competing vendors better take advantage of the reduced f in offering individual attributes, which

also benefit consumers. As a result, social welfare SW = ΠP + πL + πH + CS increases. This result

underlines the platform’s beneficial role in coordinating the vendor market through its strategic

response.

Additional analysis shows that when vendors’ development cost f declines, in equilibrium the

platform takes a larger share of the industry profit, that is, ΠP/(πL + πH) increases (see appendix

Page 23

Author: Article Short Title 23

for proof). This indicates that vendors’ technology advancement strengthens the market power

of the common platform they rely on. Our theoretical insight is consistent with the observation

of the growing power of technology platforms, as reflected by the continuous increase of their

revenue share in the digital economy (Highfill and Surfield 2022). Today, the adoption of AI tools

by reducing development cost may motivate developers to offer improved individual attributes.

Our study suggests that platforms are likely to free ride this leap in industry efficiency and enjoy

a strengthened market status in its interaction with vendors.

Meanwhile, we find that when vendors’ development cost f declines, in equilibrium although

total consumer surplus increases, its share in social welfare (i.e., CS/SW) declines (see appendix

for proof). This happens because consumers are passive decision makers, compared to the platform

that strategically sets common infrastructure as well as commission and vendors that strategically

set individual attributes and prices.

5. Model Extension

We consider extensions of the main model to demonstrate robustness and also to obtain additional

insights. All proofs are relegated to Online Appendix.

5.1. Additional platform monetization source

In addition to collecting commissions, a platform often benefits from inducing a higher sales volume,

DH + DL. For example, a higher transaction volume can bring better visibility, and consequently

attracts more users and advertisers to the platform. We capture such benefits using a stylized

expression ρ(DH + DL), with ρ ≥0 representing the marginal benefit from transaction volume

on the platform. The platform’s profit with mixed income sources can thus be written as ΠP =

α(pHDH + pLDL) + ρ(DH + DL) −λE2

equation / math rendering (image)
NOTE: contains mathematical notation; text above is the PDF text layer and symbols may be mis-extracted. Image shows the original.

2 . Our next proposition compares the platform’s optimal

strategies with and without this additional benefit from sales volume.

Proposition 5 (Platform strategies under mixed income). For a platform receiving

mixed income (i.e., ρ > 0), it provides a higher common infrastructure E and charges a higher

commission rate α than if the platform only receives commission income (i.e., ρ = 0).

Page 24

24 Author: Article Short Title

Proposition 5 suggests that the additional income from transaction volume motivates the plat-

form to offer better infrastructure so that vendors can cover more of the low-end market. Also,

the platform would increase the commission rate to further expand market coverage. The intuition

of this result stems from Proposition 2, which shows that higher commission rate disincentivizes

vendors from providing individual attributes. Prices decline as a consequence, generating a greater

sales volume for the platform. Proposition 5 confirms previous insights that the platform can

effectively combine the two strategic tools for better outcome.

It is worth noting that despite the benefit of improving platform revenue in the short term,

the platform’s strategy by raising commission rate will suppress vendor qualities. This may hurt

the platform’s reputation in the long run, although the increase of common infrastructure helps

mitigate this effect. Prior literature has shown that managing the quality of vendors’ offerings is

vital for the success of a two-sided platform (Hagiu 2009, Zheng and Kaiser 2013, Huang et al.

2022). For example, the once-dominant video game platform, Atari, collapsed after poor-quality

games flooded the market, which also led to the bankruptcy of over 90% of video game developers

(Boudreau and Hagiu 2009). Our finding suggests the platform should carefully monitor vendor

qualities (e.g., by introducing consumer reviews) when anticipating vendors adjust their individual

attributes in response to the provision and pricing of the common infrastructure.

5.2. Possible full market coverage

The main model captures the realistic situation of partial market coverage, where some low-

valuation consumers will not purchase from either of the two firms (e,g., Moorthy 1988, Choi and

Shin 1992). We now consider a model extension where full market coverage may arise in equilibrium

so that all consumers purchase a product (Gabszewicz et al. 1986). This case provides insights on

the underlying drives to findings under partial market coverage.

The model setup is similar to the main model, except that consumer quality preference θ is now

uniformly distributed on [a,b] where b > a > 0. Note that ratio b/a reflects the degree of consumer

heterogeneity (Wauthy 1996). When a = 0 and b = 1, b/a = ∞, we have the main model where the

Page 25

Author: Article Short Title 25

significant consumer heterogeneity ensures that the market is partially covered. When b ≤2a, firm

L will exit so that the market is no longer competitive. Thus, we consider b > 2a in this section.

market coverage to arise in equilibrium, where E1 = max{0, 5b3−38ab2+97a2b−136a3

erogeneity, a result consistent with the literature (Wauthy 1996). Nonetheless, desirable common

attributes E expand the region of full market coverage, as illustrated in Figure 4.

Table 1: Partial and Full Market Coverage

Figure 4: Market Coverage Regions

In this subgame, we find that the result of partial market coverage mostly extends to full market

coverage, with two differences that highlight the critical role of the low-end expansion effect in

driving the impact of common attributes in a vertically differentiated market.

First, regarding results in Proposition 1, qH no longer increases with E, whereas other results

continue to hold (i.e., the quality gap and price gap continue to increase with E; qL still decreases

with E). In particular, qH decreases with E in region (II), whereas in region (III) common attributes

have no impact on qH, and consequently limited impact on firms’ prices and demands. This is

Page 26

26 Author: Article Short Title

because under full market coverage the low-end expansion effect completely vanishes. The lacking

of demand expansion opportunities curtails firm L’s incentive to increase its price, which weakens

the surplus extraction effect. The first route of impact is thus dominated by the second route of

impact (i.e., the substitution effect).

Second, regarding results in Corollary 1, our numerical analysis shows that both the profit share

of firm L (πL/πT) and the share of consumer surplus in social welfare (CS/SW) increase with E less

rapidly compared to the case of partial market coverage, and decline when E becomes sufficiently

large. This is because under partial market coverage, the low-end expansion effect significantly

contributes to the increase of firm L’s profit and consumer surplus by converting non-buyers at the

low-end market to buyers. This benefit however no longer exists under full market coverage.

Going back to Stage 1 where the platform chooses infrastructure and commission rate, we verify

through numerical analysis that major results in Proposition 3 (corresponding to region I) extend

to regions II and III. See Supplementary Appendix for details.

6. Conclusion

This study is inspired by the prevalence of digital platforms that provide common infrastructure

to competing vendors in digital goods markets. The common infrastructure allows developers to

streamline the product development process and ensures consistency in user experience. This leads

to “common attributes” that are inseparable and indispensable from the competing products sold

through the same platform. Meanwhile, to monetize the offering of infrastructure, platforms often

charge vendors a transaction-based commission, which adds another layer of complexity in the

interactions between the platform and vendors. In this research context, we examine the interactions

between a platform and competing vendors by focusing on how the platform’s provision and pricing

of common infrastructure shape vertical competition between vendors.

Specifically, we consider a platform that offers infrastructure to a high-quality and a low-quality

vendor and charges a transaction-based fee. Our investigation renders a set of interesting results.

First, we find that when the platform offers more powerful infrastructure for the same commission

Page 27

Author: Article Short Title 27

rate, the high-quality vendor responds with improved, rather than reduced individual attributes.

Meanwhile, the low-quality firm slashes individual attributes. That is, we observe an interesting

divergence in competing vendors’ individual attributes. Moreover, improved common infrastructure

by allowing the low-quality firm to expand sales to the low-end market exert a greater impact on

the low-quality firm than on the high-quality firm, manifesting a “bottom-up” pattern of influence.

As such, improved common attributes shift the market balance in favor of the low-quality firm.

This insight is interesting because the high-quality firm is known to enjoy dominating power for

products in digital goods market. Additionally, we show that a major portion of the benefit from

more desirable common attributes is passed through to end consumers. On the other hand, when

the platform charges a higher commission for the same infrastructure, both vendors expand sales by

reducing individual attributes as well as product prices. This result highlights how the platform can

use commission rate in addition to infrastructure provision to influence vendors’ product strategies.

Second, we show that the platform will devise infrastructure strategies to support vendors’ incen-

tive to improve individual attributes when their product development cost is reduced. In particular,

the platform responds to a reduced vendor development cost with more powerful infrastructure

and lower commission, unless vendors’ development cost is already very low. In that case, further

reduction in vendors’ development cost leads to less powerful infrastructure yet lower commis-

sion rate still. These findings suggest the platform might benefit from customizing infrastructure

provision for markets with different product development efficiency.

Lastly, we show that the platform’s strategic design of infrastructure and its pricing, when

coupled with a reduced vendor development cost leads to a win-win-win outcome where all market

players including the platform itself, competing vendors, and consumers are better off. This result

highlights the critical role the platform plays in fueling the digital economy. Moreover, when the

platform benefits from sales volume in addition to commission income, the platform would always

charge a higher commission rate than if it receives commission income only.

With rapid advancements in information technology, small and innovative firms may find it ben-

eficial to leverage the powerful infrastructure of technology platforms for new product launches.

Page 28

28 Author: Article Short Title

Our research brings timely insight into quality competition in such a market environment. In prac-

tice, the platform might provide product recommendations or facilitate consumer reviews. Future

research could examine how common attributes affect these strategic platform decisions. Another

interesting topic is to study sequential product introduction. Wei and Nault (2008) considers how a

monopolist uses product versioning to deter market entry. Further research could study the quality

and price decisions of the incumbent and the entrant on a common platform.

of Lemma 2, (E∗, α∗) maximizes ΠP with the corresponding ˙r∗= r∗(E∗,α∗). We next show that

αM under mixed income (ρ > 0) is higher than α∗in the main model (ρ = 0). To facilitate the

proof, we present the following lemma (proof given later in this appendix).

Lemma A1: Given the platform’s common infrastructure E,

(i) the optimal commission rate is higher when the platform maximizes its payoff from mixed

income (ρ > 0) than when it maximizes its payoff from commission income alone (ρ = 0).

(ii) its optimal commission rate increases with E under either commission income or mixed

income.

There are two cases, which we analyze in turn.

Case 1: EM ≥E∗. We next show this condition implies αM ≥α∗. Lemma A1(ii) shows that for a

platform that offers common infrastructure E, the optimal commission rate increases with E under

mixed income. This implies that if EM ≥E∗, then αM(EM) ≥αM(E∗). Lemma A1(i) suggests that

given E∗, the commission rate under mixed income is higher than that under commission income,

i.e., αM(E∗) > α∗(E∗). Together, we obtain αM(EM) > α∗(E∗). Because (EM, αM) maximizes ΠM
